headerBody: Greece: Tourist Scams documents 65 specific scams against Greek police and consumer-protection sources — the Hellenic Police, the Tourist Police (171), and the Consumer Ombudsman — plus r/GreeceTravel reports and verified Greek news from Greek City Times, the Greek Herald, and Ekathimerini. The exact scripts, the tells that give them away, and the plain Greek phrases that shut them down. Each one is drawn as an ancient red-figure pottery scene so you recognize the setup before the pitch lands. Sourced against the record, not recycled from blog lists.
quadHead: Four ways Greece catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: The Syntagma Friendship-Bracelet & Rose
quad.tl: A man at the Syntagma metro exit grabs your wrist and loops a "friendship bracelet" before you can pull back, then demands €10–€50 — a Psyri variant presses a rose into your hand with a hug while an accomplice lifts your wallet from your back pocket. Cross your arms, step back, and walk; if it's already tied on, cut it off at a café — you owe nothing.

quad.title: The Athinios Port 'Public Bus'
quad.tl: High-vis-vest recruiters meet the Piraeus ferry at Athinios Port shouting "Public bus this way! €15 to Fira!" to disoriented arrivals — the real KTEL Santorini bus charges €2.40 for the same route and sits parked at the far end of the terminal in blue-and-white livery. Walk past the loudest voices; anything over €5 for a public-bus seat is the scam.

quad.title: The Per-Kilo Beach-Club Fish Bill
quad.tl: At a Platys Gialos beach club you order "a seabass for the table," bread and a couple of beers with no menu in sight — the bill lands at €500-plus because the fish was priced per kilogram and the "medium" one weighed 1.4 kg, with unordered bread, olives and "sparkling water" added as cover charges that Greek law actually forbids. Demand per-portion prices in writing before ordering any fish.

quad.title: The Old Town Counterfeit Market
quad.tl: Stalls along Sokratous Street sell "designer" Louis Vuitton, Gucci and Chanel bags, sunglasses and watches at €30–€150 with uneven stitching and plastic hardware — Greek customs can seize them on departure with a €1,000-plus fine, and UK or US customs seize them on arrival with no recourse. Buy souvenirs from named ceramics and leather workshops with marked provenance instead.

body: Greece: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Greek police and consumer-protection sources — the Hellenic Police, the Tourist Police (171), and the Consumer Ombudsman — plus r/GreeceTravel reports and verified Greek news from Greek City Times, the Greek Herald, and Ekathimerini. Sourced and re-reported, not recycled from blog lists.

65 specific scams across Athens, Santorini, Mykonos, Rhodes, Thessaloniki and 11 more destinations — the airport flat-rate taxi switch, the Plaka ouzeri "friendly local" trap, the per-kilo caldera fish bill, the rental-car deposit shakedown, the Syntagma bracelet. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Greek phrases that shut them down, romanized so you can read them aloud and shown in Greek script you can hold up on your phone.
Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched every year, and the current edition sits in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Greece relaxed, not braced.
